caravaggio.title: A name connected to a place
caravaggio.text: Michelangelo Merisi became known as Caravaggio, the name of the town associated with his family. His professional identity therefore carries a geographical association rather than simply preserving his family surname. That distinction helps connect the familiar name with the artist described in historical records.
caravaggio.why: Names carry histories. Recognizing this one makes biographical records easier to connect without turning the town into an explanation of the paintings.

caravaggio.title: Milan before the Roman chapels
caravaggio.text: Caravaggio trained in Milan before establishing his career in Rome. His early Roman opportunities involved the market for paintings and private support, before the major church commissions now prominent in accounts of his achievement. The public chapel painter emerged through a professional sequence, rather than appearing fully formed.
caravaggio.why: The change in audience helps explain why a private painting and a large chapel narrative make different demands on their viewers.

caravaggio.title: A cardinal’s practical support

Later public commissions extended the audience beyond the household or private collection, changing who could encounter the work and under what conditions.
caravaggio.why: Patronage concerns opportunities, introductions and audiences as well as money; it belongs to the making of a career.

caravaggio.title: A career continued through displacement
caravaggio.text: After killing a man in Rome in 1606, Caravaggio left the city. His subsequent movements included Naples, Malta and Sicily, where significant patrons continued to commission work. The documented violence is consequential, but the later paintings also belong to continuing professional relationships and changing places of production.
caravaggio.why: A dramatic life event should locate the work historically without becoming a universal explanation for every dark background or forceful gesture.

cassatt.title: An American career formed in Europe
cassatt.text: Mary Cassatt was born in Pennsylvania, but much of her professional career took shape in Europe. Study, museum encounters and working abroad were practical parts of that development. Her position connects American and French histories without making her simply a visitor to someone else’s artistic movement.
cassatt.why: The geographical distinction reveals how training and professional affiliation can differ from an artist’s birthplace.

cassatt.title: An invitation to independent exhibiting
cassatt.text: Edgar Degas invited Cassatt to exhibit with the Impressionists. She participated in several of their later independent exhibitions, entering a professional setting outside the established exhibition route. Their exchange mattered, but her subjects and compositional decisions require attention in their own right.
cassatt.why: An invitation creates an opportunity; it does not make the invited artist’s production a secondary version of the inviter’s work.

cezanne.title: Between Provence and Paris
cezanne.text: Cézanne’s career developed through movement between Provence and Paris. Encounters with contemporary artists and sustained engagement with older painting formed part of that development. The later reputation for measured construction should not erase the forceful handling and experiments associated with the earlier work.
cezanne.why: A career contains changes of circumstance and method; its later reputation need not describe every earlier painting.

cezanne.title: Repetition was a sustained investigation
cezanne.text: Cézanne repeatedly painted still lifes, portraits, landscapes and bathers. A recurring motif supplied a situation he could re-examine through altered color, spacing, viewpoint and handling. Returning to a subject did not require repeating an identical composition or treating each result as interchangeable.
cezanne.why: Repetition becomes more informative when we compare what changes within the familiar subject.

Different distances, foreground structures and conditions of appearance made the motif available for renewed investigation. Knowing the site’s name identifies a subject, but does not settle how a particular canvas organizes it.
cezanne.why: Place recognition is the beginning of a study; the particular arrangement tells us what this painting asks us to see.

dali.title: The melting watches occupy a small canvas
dali.text: The Persistence of Memory is a small oil painting, despite the monumental visibility of its image in reproduction. Its museum record makes the original dimensions available. That physical restraint matters when comparing an intimate act of close looking with the scale the picture acquires on screens and posters.
dali.why: A famous image’s cultural size and its object size are different facts, with different consequences for viewing.

dali.title: A double image carries Narcissus
dali.text: Metamorphosis of Narcissus presents a figure and a related hand-and-egg formation through comparable contours. The double image is a particular construction to examine, rather than a license to assign one fixed meaning to every object Dalí painted. Recognition itself becomes part of the viewer’s task.
dali.why: Naming the operation makes the work more approachable without pretending to solve its interpretation.

gentileschi.title: Training happened in a working studio
gentileschi.text: Artemisia Gentileschi trained in the workshop of her father, Orazio. This was practical education in the production of paintings, involving materials, composition and professional work. Her achievement was not an untrained response to later adversity; it developed within an artistic environment and an ambitious early practice.
gentileschi.why: Workshop training helps explain how artistic possibilities became available without determining every later choice.

goya.text: Goya made tapestry cartoons associated with royal decorative commissions. The Parasol belongs to that professional context, alongside a wider practice of portraits, religious subjects and prints. The later unsettling images should not be treated as though they exhaust the subjects and obligations of his career.
goya.why: Different commissions help explain the considerable differences among pictures made by the same artist.

kandinsky.title: Law preceded sustained art study
kandinsky.text: Kandinsky trained in law and economics before turning to sustained artistic study. His subsequent move to Munich placed him within another professional and cultural environment. The change of vocation is a documented development, distinct from a legend in which abstract painting simply appears without education or exchange.
kandinsky.why: A career change establishes a sequence of decisions without explaining every later painting through one turning point.

van-gogh.title: Arles included an ambition for shared work
van-gogh.text: Van Gogh’s move to Arles in 1888 involved the hope of developing a community of artists. Gauguin’s visit belonged to that project, followed by conflict and a personal crisis. The sequence matters, while the hoped-for professional community deserves attention beyond the later dramatic episode.
van-gogh.why: Artistic ambition can include the organization of a working life with others, not only the production of individual canvases.

van-gogh.title: Letters survive as a substantial source
van-gogh.text: Van Gogh’s correspondence provides dated evidence of observations, intentions and exchanges. The museum’s letters resources allow readers to distinguish his words from later popular stories. A letter addresses a particular correspondent and occasion; it need not explain every element of a painting made nearby in time.
van-gogh.why: Primary writing is most useful when its date, audience and limits remain attached to the excerpt.

vermeer.title: A Delft practice had several kinds of subject
vermeer.text: Vermeer’s work includes history painting, cityscape, domestic interiors and the tronie. The Met’s career account therefore complicates the reputation for one timeless formula of quiet rooms. Even within interiors, the depicted activity and relation to a viewer differ substantially.
vermeer.why: A familiar subject type should not become the definition of an entire professional career.

vermeer.title: A tronie is not an identified portrait
vermeer.text: The Mauritshuis classifies Girl with a Pearl Earring as a tronie. Costume and a turning head create a presence without establishing an identified sitter’s commissioned likeness. The historical category does not settle the model’s identity; it changes which claims about the image require evidence.
vermeer.why: Classification can sharpen a question without removing the figure’s persuasive human presence.

vermeer.title: Music invites context rather than a universal code
vermeer.text: The National Gallery discusses music and love as contexts for Vermeer’s virginal paintings while qualifying the suggestion that particular works were intended as a pair. Objects can support historically grounded readings, but their significance still depends on the particular composition and record.
vermeer.why: An instrument does not have one automatic meaning in every painting in which it appears.

vermeer.title: An optical hypothesis is not a complete method
vermeer.text: Proposals about Vermeer’s relationship to optical devices require evidence specific to the work and procedure being discussed. The Met’s account places technique within a practice involving selective description and compositional choice. A possible device does not make the paintings mechanically produced photographs.
vermeer.why: A technical hypothesis should explain something precisely without pretending to account for all artistic decisions.

vermeer.title: A small balance accompanies a larger image
vermeer.text: Woman Holding a Balance places a small held instrument in relation to objects on a table and a Last Judgment image behind the figure. The National Gallery of Art’s record supplies the particular work and interpretive context. The arrangement is visible; the woman’s private thought is not documented by it.
vermeer.why: Separating observation and interpretation permits a substantive ethical reading without presenting it as recovered intention.

leonardo-01.title: A portrait on wood
leonardo-01.text: Mona Lisa is painted in oil on poplar panel, rather than on canvas. The support identifies a physical object whose dimensions and surface belong to the account of the portrait. A digital enlargement does not establish the thickness or condition of its layers.
leonardo-01.why: The modest object and the enormous public image demand different kinds of attention.
leonardo-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

leonardo-01.title: The record names Lisa Gherardini
leonardo-01.text: The Louvre identifies the sitter as Lisa Gherardini, wife of Francesco del Giocondo. That identification is a historical claim grounded in the collection record. A description of her expression as welcoming, reserved or amused is a different kind of statement.
leonardo-01.why: A named sitter does not make the image a recovered account of her private feelings.
leonardo-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

leonardo-01.title: A royal painting entered the museum’s records in 1793
leonardo-01.text: The Louvre records the Mona Lisa as coming from the former royal collection, with an acquisition date of 1793. The date marks an institutional stage in the painting’s history, rather than the year it was made.
leonardo-01.why: A secure later history can coexist with questions about earlier custody.
leonardo-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.
leonardo-01.evidenceNote: The acquisition field concerns the museum record. It does not independently document every transfer from Leonardo’s possession.

leonardo-01.title: The hands establish a visible base
leonardo-01.text: Overlapping hands occupy the foreground beneath the turned upper body. Their comparatively legible boundaries can be compared with the softer transitions around mouth and cheek. This describes the image’s arrangement; the claim that the contrast makes the face seem responsive is an interpretation.
leonardo-01.why: Separating an observable relationship from its proposed effect gives another viewer a way to test the reading.
leonardo-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

leonardo-01.title: Celebrity is a later condition of viewing
leonardo-01.text: The portrait’s present museum fame belongs to an afterlife involving collecting, reproduction and public attention. The original portrait encounter and the crowded encounter with an icon are different conditions. Familiarity alone does not reveal what an early viewer understood in the face.
leonardo-01.why: Recognizing a work immediately is not the same as having examined the particular painted relationships.
leonardo-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

leonardo-02.title: A meal painted for a refectory
leonardo-02.text: The Last Supper occupies a wall of the Dominican refectory at Santa Maria delle Grazie. The represented meal therefore addressed a community using the room for meals. The painted table and the historical dining space belong to one original architectural encounter.
leonardo-02.why: The setting gives a concrete reason to consider the spectator’s relation to the meal.
leonardo-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

leonardo-02.title: An experimental dry-wall technique
leonardo-02.text: Leonardo used an experimental method on a dry surface rather than executing the entire work in conventional buon fresco. The museum’s conservation account is essential to understanding its survival. The material distinction helps explain why present appearance and original execution cannot be assumed identical.
leonardo-02.why: Technique has consequences for preservation as well as for the effects the painter could pursue.
leonardo-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

leonardo-02.title: Sforza patronage forms part of its setting
leonardo-02.text: The mural belongs to the context of Ludovico Sforza’s patronage in Milan. Its religious institution, courtly support and communal use are connected circumstances. It was not originally a movable canvas produced for a modern museum’s sequence of masterpieces.
leonardo-02.why: Commissioning relationships locate artistic invention within a particular professional and institutional world.
leonardo-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

leonardo-02.title: Its journey is a building’s history
leonardo-02.text: Unlike a portable easel painting, this work’s later history concerns a wall, room and building. Damage and conservation are central stages rather than a succession of ordinary market sales. Documented treatment must distinguish surviving original material from later intervention.
leonardo-02.why: A painting’s journey need not be a list of owners; the form of the object determines which events matter.
leonardo-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

leonardo-02.title: Copies preserve different evidence
leonardo-02.text: Copies helped transmit the composition’s grouping under circumstances unlike those of the original wall. A copy can preserve information about arrangement while changing color, scale, handling and viewing conditions. It remains a separate object with its own authorship and history.
leonardo-02.why: A related image is useful evidence when its differences and limitations stay visible.
leonardo-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

rembrandt-01.title: A commission for a civic company
rembrandt-01.text: The portrait was commissioned for a civic guard company associated with Captain Frans Banning Cocq. Its social purpose involved representing a paid group and its standing. The apparent action is a composition constructed for that purpose, rather than an unplanned image of soldiers caught assembling.
rembrandt-01.why: Unequal illumination and prominence acquire significance within the obligations of group representation.
rembrandt-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

rembrandt-01.title: The canvas was cut down in 1715
rembrandt-01.text: The painting moved from the Kloveniersdoelen to Amsterdam’s town hall in 1715 and was cut down for the new setting. Its surviving edges are therefore part of a later physical history. The current rectangle does not reproduce the composition’s full original extent.
rembrandt-01.why: Following a figure toward an edge also becomes a question about what no longer survives there.

rembrandt-01.title: An early copy records a wider arrangement
rembrandt-01.text: A copy attributed to Gerrit Lundens provides evidence for parts of the original arrangement lost through trimming. It is a distinct painting, rather than recovered Rembrandt paint. The visual comparison should identify both objects and avoid implying that the copy reproduces every original color or surface effect exactly.
rembrandt-01.why: Reconstruction depends on evidence whose strengths and limits can be examined separately.

rembrandt-01.title: The Night Watch was a later name
rembrandt-01.text: The Night Watch is a later familiar title, not the wording of the original commission. It should not be used on its own to establish the represented time of day. Titles can shape an encounter while belonging to a different historical moment from the making.
rembrandt-01.why: A name that feels inseparable from a picture may still be evidence of its later reception.
rembrandt-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

rembrandt-01.title: A very large group portrait
rembrandt-01.text: The recorded canvas measures several meters in both directions. Its bodies and interrupted lines of sight therefore address the spectator differently from a small reproduction. Fitting it to a screen preserves relative positions while reducing the bodily scale of the encounter.
rembrandt-01.why: Physical dimensions help explain why movement and overlap matter beyond the identification of individual faces.
rembrandt-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

vermeer-01.title: A tronie rather than a named commission
vermeer-01.text: The Mauritshuis classifies the painting as a tronie: a study of a figure or character rather than a securely identified sitter’s commissioned portrait. The headdress and ornament contribute to that presentation. No original patron or named model should be supplied simply to complete a story.
vermeer-01.why: The historical category changes the question without diminishing the figure’s persuasive presence.

vermeer-01.title: The Girl resurfaced at an auction in 1881
vermeer-01.text: Andries des Tombe bought Girl with a Pearl Earring at a Hague auction in 1881; his bequest brought it to the Mauritshuis in 1903. The museum’s provenance distinguishes that secure modern history from uncertain proposals about the painting’s earlier owners.
vermeer-01.why: Secure dates are most valuable when the untraced interval remains explicit.

vermeer-01.title: A few bright marks suggest an ornament
vermeer-01.text: The hanging ornament is represented through abbreviated light accents and surrounding darker passages. Its apparent substance is an effect of the painted relationships. Calling it a pearl in the title does not by itself identify the material of an actual object worn by a model.
vermeer-01.why: A compelling illusion and a verified material identification need different evidence.

vermeer-01.title: The background has a material history
vermeer-01.text: Mauritshuis technical research reports evidence relevant to the original background, including a curtain. The present darkness should not be treated as a transparent record of the painting’s first appearance. Research on paint alteration addresses a different question from identifying the sitter.
vermeer-01.why: Material findings can change a visual account without settling an unrelated biographical uncertainty.

vermeer-01.title: The original is a small canvas
vermeer-01.text: The painting is roughly forty-five centimeters high, rather than a monumental head conceived at poster scale. Its compact dimensions belong to the physical encounter recorded by the museum. A large screen image can make the face familiar under quite different conditions.
vermeer-01.why: Knowing the scale helps separate cultural prominence from the size of the work itself.

van-gogh-01.title: A Saint-Rémy painting of 1889
van-gogh-01.text: The Starry Night belongs to Van Gogh’s Saint-Rémy period in 1889. The institutional account places it within a specific working situation. It should not be treated as a direct clinical record, or as proof that every depicted feature was observed from one window at one instant.
van-gogh-01.why: A date and setting establish circumstances without determining the meaning of every painted mark.

source.title: Museum of Modern Art · The Starry Night

van-gogh-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

van-gogh-01.title: The Starry Night entered MoMA through an exchange
van-gogh-01.text: MoMA acquired The Starry Night in 1941 through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest, by exchange. The credit describes a museum acquisition mechanism, not a direct gift from the painter.
van-gogh-01.why: Acquisition wording explains how a museum obtained an object, not simply who is associated with its image.

source.title: Museum of Modern Art · The Starry Night

van-gogh-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.
van-gogh-01.evidenceNote: The collection credit and acquisition record establish this museum stage. They are not a complete chain of ownership.

van-gogh-01.title: Village and sky have different marks
van-gogh-01.text: The roofs and settlement can be compared with curved bands and repeated directions in the sky. The visible difference is available to inspect without diagnosing the painter. An account of how the contrast creates intensity is an argument about the arrangement.
van-gogh-01.why: Observation becomes more precise when it names which marks differ and where that difference occurs.

source.title: Museum of Modern Art · The Starry Night

van-gogh-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

van-gogh-01.title: A cypress crosses the distant field
van-gogh-01.text: The dark cypress rises in the foreground across the space occupied by village and sky. Its position gives a particular relationship to follow from near to far. The tree’s role in a symbolic interpretation requires additional argument beyond recognizing what it depicts.
van-gogh-01.why: A prominent form can have a compositional function before it is assigned a fixed symbolic meaning.

source.title: Museum of Modern Art · The Starry Night

van-gogh-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

van-gogh-01.title: Reproduction changes the surface encounter
van-gogh-01.text: The original is an oil painting with visible directional handling. Reproductions can transmit its broad arrangement while changing scale, luminosity and the perception of surface relief. A bright display does not reproduce how ambient light meets the canvas and its paint.
van-gogh-01.why: A familiar digital image is a useful route to the work, with physical limits worth knowing.

leonardo-06.title: Ginevra’s portrait has a painted reverse
leonardo-06.text: Ginevra de’ Benci is a double-sided painted panel. The portrait’s reverse carries an emblematic design, so a reproduction of the face alone omits part of the physical object. The museum’s presentation allows the sides to be considered together without treating them as separate unrelated works.
leonardo-06.why: The object’s two-sided structure complicates the apparently self-contained frontal encounter.

source.title: National Gallery of Art · Ginevra de’ Benci

leonardo-06.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

leonardo-06.title: The lower extent has changed
leonardo-06.text: The panel has been cut down. Its present lower edge cannot simply stand for the full original composition. A proposed reconstruction should therefore remain distinct from what physically survives and should identify the evidence used to suggest the missing extent.
leonardo-06.why: An image can feel complete while the history of its support records alteration.

source.title: National Gallery of Art · Ginevra de’ Benci

leonardo-06.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

leonardo-06.title: Ginevra crossed from a princely collection to Washington
leonardo-06.text: The National Gallery of Art purchased Ginevra de’ Benci from the Liechtenstein collection in 1967. The museum’s provenance records a secure acquisition date while qualifying parts of the earlier ownership history.
leonardo-06.why: An acquisition date helps locate the modern audience within a longer object history.

source.title: National Gallery of Art · Ginevra de’ Benci

leonardo-06.evidenceNote: The NGA records purchase on 10 February 1967. Earlier ownership is described with different levels of certainty; those qualifications should not be removed.

leonardo-06.title: Juniper accompanies an identified sitter
leonardo-06.text: The portrait presents the identified Ginevra de’ Benci before juniper foliage. Associations between the name, vegetation and reverse have been discussed in scholarship. The visible plant can support inquiry, but it does not independently prove one complete account of a marriage or personal relationship.
leonardo-06.why: A recognizable motif needs historical support before becoming a decisive biographical explanation.

leonardo-06.title: The present object is nearly square
leonardo-06.text: The surviving panel’s recorded height and width are close to one another. Those dimensions concern the altered object now encountered. The compressed head-and-foliage arrangement should therefore be distinguished from a confident reconstruction of the portrait’s complete original framing.
leonardo-06.why: The museum’s measurements describe what survives, a necessary starting point for discussing what may be missing.

source.title: National Gallery of Art · Ginevra de’ Benci

michelangelo-02.title: A fresco above the spectator
michelangelo-02.text: The Creation of Adam is fresco within the Sistine Chapel ceiling. It was made for an architectural field viewed from below, not as an independent easel painting. Neighboring scenes and the viewer’s bodily position belong to its original presentation.
michelangelo-02.why: The upward encounter changes how monumental bodies and a small interval operate together.
michelangelo-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

michelangelo-02.title: Julius II supplied the commission’s setting
michelangelo-02.text: The scene belongs to the ceiling commission under Pope Julius II. That patronal setting connects the painter’s work to a larger scriptural program and papal institution. The celebrated detail of the reaching hands is one part of those historical circumstances.
michelangelo-02.why: A commission provides purpose and context beyond a famous isolated motif.
michelangelo-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

michelangelo-02.title: The famous fingertips remain apart
michelangelo-02.text: The two extended hands do not meet. The narrow interval is visibly prepared by larger bodies in different positions: a grounded recline and an approaching group. Describing that arrangement is distinct from claiming the fresco records an actual instant of contact.
michelangelo-02.why: A familiar emblem can obscure the physical separation that makes the whole composition worth reconsidering.
michelangelo-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

michelangelo-02.title: The original remains in its chapel
michelangelo-02.text: The fresco remains in the Sistine Chapel. Its later history therefore concerns the building’s use, conservation and reproduction rather than a normal sequence of private sales. Restoration images need dates and institutional descriptions to distinguish documented states.
michelangelo-02.why: The history of access and surface can matter more than a conventional ownership list.
michelangelo-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

michelangelo-02.title: An anatomical resemblance is a hypothesis
michelangelo-02.text: Proposals identifying anatomical structures within the surrounding forms should be attributed and supported. A visible similarity can be described, but it does not establish Vatican-confirmed intention or a complete hidden code. Evidence of design or contemporary explanation would address a different level of claim.
michelangelo-02.why: An interesting hypothesis becomes stronger through evidence, not through the frequency with which it is repeated.
michelangelo-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

raphael-01.title: Ancient philosophy in papal apartments
raphael-01.text: The School of Athens belongs to Julius II’s Vatican apartments and a wider arrangement of knowledge. Ancient philosophers appear within a Christian patron’s program. The gathering is an imagined assembly, not a record of people who all met together historically.
raphael-01.why: The apparent community has an institutional purpose as well as an intellectual subject.
raphael-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

raphael-01.title: The wall extends an architectural room
raphael-01.text: The fresco’s painted architecture interacts with the Stanza della Segnatura’s real setting. Reproducing it as an isolated rectangle preserves the composition while removing its relation to other walls and subjects. The room, rather than the image alone, provides the original ensemble.
raphael-01.why: Architecture helps establish how the painting’s order is encountered and what it belongs beside.
raphael-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

raphael-01.title: Not every figure has an equally secure name
raphael-01.text: Plato and Aristotle have comparatively secure conventional identifications, while the identification of several peripheral figures remains disputed. A likeness to a contemporary person does not independently establish an ancient philosopher’s identity. Different levels of certainty should not be presented as equivalent catalogue facts.
raphael-01.why: Recognizing uncertainty leaves room for close analysis even when a proposed name remains unsettled.
raphael-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

raphael-01.title: Learning is depicted in local groups
raphael-01.text: Beyond the central pair, figures read, converse and attend to a diagram. Those visible activities distribute attention across smaller groups. The identification of every participant is not required to compare solitary, conversational and demonstrative forms of inquiry within the arrangement.
raphael-01.why: The margins contribute intellectual activity rather than merely supplying a frame for famous central identities.
raphael-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

raphael-01.title: A drawing would be a different object
raphael-01.text: A related cartoon or preparatory drawing represents a distinct stage and physical object, not an alternative photograph of the fresco. Its material, extent and history require their own record. Comparing it with the wall can illuminate decisions only when those differences stay identified.
raphael-01.why: Preparatory evidence is useful because it differs from the finished work, not because it is interchangeable with it.
raphael-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

caravaggio-02.title: A private patron commissioned the Emmaus encounter
caravaggio-02.text: Ciriaco Mattei commissioned the London Supper at Emmaus in 1601. Its first setting belonged to an elite private collection, giving this biblical encounter a different audience from Caravaggio’s public chapel paintings.
caravaggio-02.why: Private devotion and public chapel viewing are different audiences for an apparently immediate religious event.
caravaggio-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.
caravaggio-02.evidenceNote: The National Gallery identifies Mattei and the 1601 painting. The audience comparison is an editorial explanation of the difference between private collecting and public installation.

caravaggio-02.title: London and Milan are distinct versions
caravaggio-02.text: This study concerns the 1601 London painting, not Caravaggio’s later Emmaus composition in Milan. The two works have different dates and arrangements. The later painting is not an earlier state uncovered beneath this canvas or a substitute for its object record.
caravaggio-02.why: Version precision prevents histories and technical findings from migrating between separate paintings.
caravaggio-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

caravaggio-02.title: The Emmaus canvas reached the National Gallery in 1839
caravaggio-02.text: The National Gallery acquired the London Supper at Emmaus in 1839. Its catalogue follows the painting through earlier collections, separating that museum arrival from the Mattei commission.
caravaggio-02.why: A museum acquisition changes access to an object without explaining its entire preceding life.
caravaggio-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.
caravaggio-02.evidenceNote: This is the London object record. The acquisition date must not be attached to Caravaggio’s later Emmaus painting in Milan.

caravaggio-02.title: A basket projects past the table
caravaggio-02.text: The basket approaches and overhangs the table’s apparent edge. Its relation to reaching arms, food and chair can be observed before it is interpreted as involving the spectator in recognition. The painted projection does not require inventing a literal place assigned to the viewer at the meal.
caravaggio-02.why: A small ordinary object can help organize the relationship between represented room and viewing space.
caravaggio-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

caravaggio-02.title: The canvas has a broad horizontal reach
caravaggio-02.text: The painting is approximately two meters wide. Its extended table and outward gestures therefore occupy a bodily scale that a small screen compresses. The recorded dimensions concern the actual canvas; a fitted image preserves proportion while changing the distance and reach of the encounter.
caravaggio-02.why: Physical scale makes the question of projection more than an optical trick in a small illustration.
caravaggio-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

rembrandt-02.title: A surgeons’ guild commission
rembrandt-02.text: The 1632 commission belongs to Amsterdam’s surgeons’ guild and the professional standing of Nicolaes Tulp. The painting therefore has a social function as a group portrait alongside its subject of demonstration. The participants’ presence and visibility are part of that professional representation.
rembrandt-02.why: Knowing the commissioning context changes the question from what is being taught to who is being represented.
rembrandt-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

rembrandt-02.title: The body has a documented identity
rembrandt-02.text: The body represented is associated with the executed Aris Kindt. The instructional scene therefore rests on a legal and social inequality as well as a professional occasion. Naming the subject does not make every painted anatomical relation a transparent report of a single demonstration.
rembrandt-02.why: A person who cannot return the gaze should not disappear behind the reputation of the lecturer and group.
rembrandt-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

rembrandt-02.title: A demonstrator’s hands organize attention
rembrandt-02.text: The lecturer’s hands and the participants’ different lines of sight distribute looking across the scene. A book and exposed forearm contribute to its instructional arrangement. Those elements can be observed separately from the assumption that every participant looked exactly this way at one historical instant.
rembrandt-02.why: A composed demonstration can make knowledge legible while also staging professional authority.
rembrandt-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

rembrandt-02.title: A planned sale ended with state acquisition
rembrandt-02.text: The Dutch State acquired The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp in 1828 and placed it in the Mauritshuis. The museum’s provenance records the intervention that stopped a planned sale by the surgeons’ widows’ fund.
rembrandt-02.why: An object’s audience can change even when its subject remains the same.
rembrandt-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.
rembrandt-02.evidenceNote: The provenance distinguishes the surgeons’ guild, the widows’ fund and the state acquisition. It supports more than a general statement that the painting eventually entered a museum.

rembrandt-02.title: An anatomy image is also a paid portrait
rembrandt-02.text: The work’s familiar subject can overshadow its role as commissioned group portraiture. The men are made recognizable while their attention is organized around the demonstration. The two functions coexist; treating the picture only as an anatomical illustration misses the social work performed by its arrangement.
rembrandt-02.why: A painting can communicate knowledge and membership through the same distribution of bodies and light.
rembrandt-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

vermeer-05.title: The balance’s pans are empty
vermeer-05.text: The National Gallery of Art’s discussion identifies the balance as empty. The tiny instrument should not be described as visibly carrying coins or jewels simply because such objects appear nearby. Its suspended condition changes the account of what action the painting represents.
vermeer-05.why: A small object fact can alter an entire interpretation of value, judgment and the timing of an act.

vermeer-05.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

vermeer-05.title: A Last Judgment hangs behind the figure
vermeer-05.text: A picture of the Last Judgment occupies the wall behind the woman. Its presence is part of the composition’s documented subject matter. The relationship between that image and the foreground balance supports interpretation, but does not recover the sitter’s private religious thought.
vermeer-05.why: A painting within a painting supplies context that still needs to be related carefully to the visible action.

vermeer-05.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

vermeer-05.title: An original patron is not supplied
vermeer-05.text: The original patron is not securely identified in this study. An affluent interior and a religious image do not independently establish a purchaser’s identity or beliefs. The National Gallery of Art’s record, rather than a plausible story about ownership, should govern a more complete account.
vermeer-05.why: An explicit gap is more useful than a confident but unsupported commissioning narrative.

vermeer-05.title: The Widener credit names a collection stage
vermeer-05.text: The museum’s Widener Collection credit provides a secure institutional context. Earlier descriptions and provenance require catalogue distinctions, including cases where a historical description could refer to more than one work. The collection credit should not be expanded into an invented uninterrupted chain.
vermeer-05.why: A specific acquisition context and a complete earlier provenance are different levels of documentation.

vermeer-05.title: Published interpretations differ
vermeer-05.text: The NGA catalogue discusses readings associated with Rudolph, Swillens and Gowing, including vanitas, practical adjustment and the weighing of souls. These attributed positions belong to the work’s interpretive history. They are not interchangeable statements of what Vermeer privately intended.
vermeer-05.why: An actual disagreement is most useful when its visible and documentary points of difference can be identified.

gentileschi-02.title: Painting has a female personification
gentileschi-02.text: The work engages the tradition of personifying Painting as a woman, associated with Cesare Ripa’s account. The Royal Collection connects this visual language with Gentileschi’s self-representation. It supplies a particular historical context for the meeting of professional identity and allegorical figure.
gentileschi-02.why: The painter’s identity can operate within an established convention while also changing how it is encountered.

gentileschi-02.title: The body is shown at work
gentileschi-02.text: The turning head, angled torso and working arm make activity part of the image’s subject. That visible arrangement supports a professional claim, while it does not document an unposed instant in the actual studio. A painted pose is a constructed account of labor.
gentileschi-02.why: Depicting work involves choices about how a spectator understands the activity and the person undertaking it.

gentileschi-02.title: The work belongs to the English period
gentileschi-02.text: The painting is associated with Gentileschi’s English period and royal collecting. That setting supplies a historical relationship without independently establishing every detail of the original commission or payment. The Royal Collection record is the starting point for distinctions among association, provenance and documented contract.
gentileschi-02.why: A courtly context should not become an invented account of a patron’s exact instructions.

gentileschi-02.text: Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting combines a claim about likeness with a claim about personification. Those are related but distinct aspects of the collection’s identification. How literally the likeness functions and how each attribute follows convention remain questions for close study.
gentileschi-02.why: A title can provide a historically grounded framework while still leaving consequential interpretation open.

gentileschi-02.title: The original is a substantial upright canvas
gentileschi-02.text: The canvas is approximately a meter high and three-quarters of a meter wide. Those dimensions belong to the Royal Collection’s object record. Its active body occupies a scale a small reproduction can disguise; the turned pose is more than a miniature emblem of a profession.
gentileschi-02.why: Scale gives the account of labor a bodily presence alongside its allegorical significance.

goya-01.title: Made six years after the represented event
goya-01.text: The Third of May 1808 was painted in 1814. The gap separates the event commemorated from the making of its image. The canvas constructs remembrance after the violence; it is not proof that Goya personally witnessed every represented incident.
goya-01.why: Chronology matters to how we discuss testimony, memory and the authority of a history painting.

goya-01.title: A postwar commemorative project
goya-01.text: The painting belongs to a project of remembrance after the war. Its relationship to official commemoration matters even when its arrangement resists a comfortable celebration of state authority. The historical purpose and later broader antiwar readings should not simply be collapsed into one moment.
goya-01.why: A public commission can produce an image whose effects exceed a single official account.

source.title: Museo del Prado · The 3rd of May 1808

goya-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

goya-01.title: Several moments of violence coexist
goya-01.text: Bodies lie in the foreground, a group faces the rifles and other figures wait. These visible positions bring aftermath, present action and anticipated violence into one arrangement. They should be examined before an interpretation concentrates exclusively on the central raised arms.
goya-01.why: The image’s account of time depends on more than its most reproduced figure.

goya-01.title: The executioners repeat a posture
goya-01.text: The soldiers’ backs and aimed weapons form a repeated line, while the faces and gestures opposite them vary. The opposition is visible in the canvas. Describing it as the confrontation of mechanism and individuality is an editorial argument grounded in that arrangement.
goya-01.why: Observation makes a strong interpretation discussable rather than merely emphatic.

goya-01.title: The central victim is not securely named here
goya-01.text: The recognizable pose does not independently establish the central victim’s identity. Christian associations may illuminate the extended arms, but an analogy does not prove one exclusive symbolic program. The Prado record should guide historical identification separately from interpretive proposals.
goya-01.why: A compelling association remains stronger when it does not claim certainty that the evidence cannot supply.

turner-01.title: The title remembers 1838; the exhibition came in 1839
turner-01.text: The Temeraire’s final journey took place in 1838; Turner exhibited his painting at the Royal Academy in 1839. The National Gallery catalogue keeps the event, the title and the exhibition chronology distinct.
turner-01.why: Two neighboring dates can answer different historical questions rather than contradict one another.
turner-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.
turner-01.evidenceNote: Use the object catalogue and exhibition record for the distinction. An abbreviated institutional report may reproduce the title’s 1838 as though it were the painting date.

turner-01.title: The voyage was imaginatively reconstructed
turner-01.text: The National Gallery describes Turner’s departures from the ship’s actual journey and appearance. The picture is an imaginative construction using historical material, rather than a mechanically exact report of the tow. Its poetic alterations should be discussed without replacing the documented circumstances.
turner-01.why: Accuracy and invention become more interesting when the specific differences are named.
turner-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

turner-01.title: A contested bequest delayed the national collection
turner-01.text: The Fighting Temeraire entered the national collection through the Turner Bequest in 1856. Turner had died in 1851; legal disputes delayed the settlement, so the bequest date is not the artist’s year of death.
turner-01.why: The absence of a conventional sales sequence is itself important to this object’s institutional history.
turner-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.
turner-01.evidenceNote: The painting’s provenance supplies 1856; the National Gallery’s bequest history explains the interval after Turner’s death.

turner-01.title: Reviewers encountered it in 1839
turner-01.text: The painting was exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1839, where the National Gallery records favorable responses to its poetic and patriotic associations. That early reception is distinct from its subsequent popularity in a national collection and its present status as a familiar image.
turner-01.why: A famous afterlife should not be used as evidence that every audience valued the painting in the same way.
turner-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

turner-01.title: The tug performs the depicted labor
turner-01.text: The small dark tug supplies the motion of the ship’s departure, while the pale warship carries a different visual scale and historical identity. These are observable relations. Whether the machine appears threatening, necessary or both remains a reading to test against the whole arrangement.
turner-01.why: The painting’s relationship to technological change is more complex than a simple opposition between a hero and a villain.
turner-01.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

monet-02.title: Camille and Jean are identified
monet-02.text: The figures are identified as Camille Monet and their son Jean. Their participation belongs to a family and working context, while the painting’s arrangement remains constructed for a spectator. Identification does not by itself establish a paid commission or the sitters’ private response.
monet-02.why: Knowing who is depicted should enrich looking without replacing an account of how they are painted.

monet-02.title: The spectator looks from below
monet-02.text: A low viewpoint places the main figure against the sky, with grass rising in the foreground. The recorded arrangement differs from an evenly lit indoor portrait. The parasol, fabric and surrounding air participate in how the figure becomes visible.
monet-02.why: Viewpoint can make a recognizable sitter belong to an unstable outdoor encounter.

monet-02.title: Lively marks do not time the entire execution
monet-02.text: Visible handling in the dress, grass and sky can produce a sensation of a passing moment. That appearance does not establish that the whole canvas was completed without revision or in one uninterrupted session. A working chronology requires different evidence.
monet-02.why: An impression of speed is an artistic effect, not a stopwatch reading.

monet-02.title: The Mellon collection is a documented stage
monet-02.text: The National Gallery of Art acquired the painting through the Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon. The collection credit supplies a particular museum context. A subject depicting the artist’s family should not be mistaken for evidence of an unbroken family ownership chain.
monet-02.why: Subject matter and provenance answer different questions about the same object.

monet-02.title: Its height is about a meter
monet-02.text: The original canvas is approximately a meter high. The figure’s relationship to the viewer therefore differs from that of a small image on a phone. The recorded dimensions help distinguish the scale of the painted encounter from the ease with which the image circulates.
monet-02.why: A familiar outdoor scene can involve a more substantial bodily presence than its reproduction suggests.

morisot-02.title: A boating scene dated about 1879
morisot-02.text: The National Gallery dates Summer’s Day to about 1879. The painting’s cropped boat and separate gazes make a modern leisure scene into a carefully organized encounter.
morisot-02.why: The occasion represented should not be confused with the conditions of making the work.
morisot-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.
morisot-02.evidenceNote: The institutional date is approximate. The proposed importance of cropping and gaze is an editorial reading, not a documented account of the sitters’ thoughts.

morisot-02.title: The boat’s boundary cuts the view
morisot-02.text: The curved boat edge and cropped arrangement put the spectator close to the figures. Water is represented through broken marks rather than an evenly described scenic background. These visible decisions define a restricted viewpoint before any emotional explanation of the encounter is proposed.
morisot-02.why: The frame actively shapes access rather than merely enclosing a pleasant subject.
morisot-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

morisot-02.title: One bequest links two cities’ collections
morisot-02.text: Summer’s Day carries the credit Sir Hugh Lane Bequest, 1917, The National Gallery, London. The bequest’s history includes disputed testamentary wishes and later sharing arrangements with Dublin.
morisot-02.why: Institutional history can be more complicated than the single museum name beside an image.
morisot-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.
morisot-02.evidenceNote: The 1917 credit is a collection-history designation, not Lane’s death date. The ownership and loan history should be checked separately from current display.

morisot-02.title: A catalogue title does not identify every lake scene
morisot-02.text: The relationship of a particular exhibition title to this canvas requires the National Gallery’s object discussion. A historic catalogue mentioning a lake or boating scene is not automatically evidence for this exact painting. Identifying the object precedes reconstructing its reception.
morisot-02.why: A plausible subject match still needs documentary support before becoming an exhibition fact.
morisot-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

morisot-02.title: The figures do not form one expression
morisot-02.text: The two figures’ directions of attention can be examined separately. Their proximity does not establish a shared mood or disclose what each was thinking. The broken water and close frame also contribute to the encounter rather than functioning as neutral scenery.
morisot-02.why: A scene can be immediate while leaving its human relationship unresolved.
morisot-02.reviewScope: Editorial comparison with the existing cited collection account; not a claim of new independent primary research.

cassatt-01.title: A high viewpoint organizes the bath
cassatt-01.text: The Child’s Bath is viewed from above, bringing bodies, basin and patterned surfaces into a compressed arrangement. The Art Institute’s account relates the work to Cassatt’s artistic investigation. The composition offers a particular spatial decision to examine rather than a generic illustration of maternal affection.
cassatt-01.why: Viewpoint changes which contacts become visible and how the surrounding pattern participates.

cassatt-01.title: The title does not identify mother and child
cassatt-01.text: A gesture of care is depicted, but the exact identities and relationship of the models are separate historical questions. The picture is not evidence that Cassatt represented her own motherhood. No named family should be supplied merely because the scene looks intimate.
cassatt-01.why: Constructed intimacy can have artistic authority without becoming an invented family biography.

cassatt-01.title: A named fund brought the painting to Chicago
cassatt-01.text: The Art Institute acquired The Child’s Bath in 1910 through the Robert A. Waller Fund. Its museum credit identifies the means and year of entry into the collection.
cassatt-01.why: Acquisition history connects an intimate subject with its later public life.

cassatt-01.title: Japanese prints provide a specific context
cassatt-01.text: Japanese prints are a documented context for Cassatt’s attention to viewpoint and pattern. Their relevance should be explained through particular conventions and encounters, rather than an anonymous claim that the composition looks Eastern. Influence is a historical relationship requiring precision.
cassatt-01.why: Naming a context responsibly makes comparison more useful and avoids turning a tradition into a vague stylistic label.

cassatt-01.title: Contact interrupts the patterned field
cassatt-01.text: Hands and the child’s foot form specific contacts amid stripes and surrounding pattern. Their arrangement remains visible even where space is compressed. An interpretation of care can begin with those points of support rather than assuming that the subject alone guarantees the emotional effect.
cassatt-01.why: The difference between pattern and touch helps explain how the painting makes an ordinary task compelling.

cezanne-01.title: The table has incompatible continuities
cezanne-01.text: The table edge on either side of the white cloth does not resolve into an effortless continuous alignment. The Art Institute’s discussion makes that difficulty available for examination. Describing the visible mismatch is distinct from reconstructing Cézanne’s actual eye movements or every stage of execution.
cezanne-01.why: An object can look convincing while the common support beneath it remains difficult to explain.

cezanne-01.title: Ordinary objects occupy an ambitious picture
cezanne-01.text: The arrangement contains apples, a basket, a bottle, cloth and biscuits. The still-life subject does not require a rare collection of possessions or a documented grand commission to sustain serious pictorial investigation. The status of its first purchaser remains a separate historical question.
cezanne-01.why: Ambition can reside in the relationships among familiar things rather than the prestige of the depicted subject.

cezanne-01.text: Different tilts can be observed in the table, bottle and dish. Those appearances do not independently establish the order of revisions or the artist’s stated reason for changing a form. Material investigation and documentary evidence would address that additional question.
cezanne-01.why: A persuasive formal explanation should not be presented as an observed record of the making process.

cezanne-01.title: The fruit retains its apparent weight
cezanne-01.text: The apples remain recognizable and can appear substantial amid the unsettled supporting edges. That visible coexistence gives the viewer a concrete problem to explore. cezanne-01.why: A good interpretation explains both the painting’s coherence and its difficulty, rather than only one side of the encounter.

van-gogh-02.title: A major Nuenen composition of 1885
van-gogh-02.text: The Potato Eaters belongs to Van Gogh’s Nuenen work in 1885. It was an ambitious professional statement, not a securely identified paid commission in this study. The dark palette and group arrangement deserve attention as choices within that early ambition.
van-gogh-02.why: An early painting can be judged through its particular aims rather than treated as a deficient version of later color.

van-gogh-02.text: On 30 April 1885, Van Gogh wrote to Theo about the labor he wanted the hands in The Potato Eaters to convey. The letter also describes a winter of preparatory work behind a canvas painted over a much shorter period.
van-gogh-02.why: Primary evidence becomes stronger when its author, recipient, occasion and limits remain attached.

van-gogh-02.why: The argument about dignity depends on arrangement as well as the identity of the subject.

van-gogh-02.text: The museum’s account locates the canvas within the artist’s family and foundation collection history. That route should not be replaced by a speculative sequence of market sales. The present Van Gogh Museum setting is one documented destination within that particular history.
van-gogh-02.why: Not every famous painting reaches a museum through the same collecting mechanism.

kandinsky-02.title: A work of the Bauhaus period
kandinsky-02.text: Composition VIII dates from 1923, during Kandinsky’s Bauhaus years. The work’s numbered title identifies a specific painting, not a universal formula for the period.
kandinsky-02.why: A historical setting can inform interpretation without dictating the function of every shape.

kandinsky-02.why: A title can organize a body of work while leaving the particular arrangement open to looking.

kandinsky-02.title: Open areas are visible elements of the field
kandinsky-02.text: Circles, diagonals and angular groups appear alongside substantial open intervals. The pale spaces separate forms and alter their apparent emphasis. Describing those relations does not require assigning every shape a hidden object name or fixed musical note.
kandinsky-02.why: What is left open can matter as much as the number of shapes present.

kandinsky-02.text: Kandinsky’s theoretical writing provides evidence for ideas developed within a changing practice. kandinsky-02.why: Keeping dates and purposes attached to theory makes it useful rather than prescriptive.
